¶ '''bearing-cloth''' (bãr′ing-klôth), ''n.'' The cloth with which a child is covered when carried to church to be baptized. Also called ''bear-cloth.'' {{smaller block|Thy scarlet robes, as a child’s ''bearing-cloth,''
I’ll use to carry thee out of this place. {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., i. 3.}}}} '''bearing-feeler''' (bãr′ing-fē″lėr), ''n.'' An automatic alarm for signaling the overheating of a journal-bearing. {{smaller|A plug of fusible material connected with the bearing melts at a given temperature, and by suitable connections is made to sound an alarm.}} '''bearing-neck''' (bãr′ing-nek), ''n.'' The part which turns within the brasses of the pedestal of a car-truck, and sustains the strain; the journal of a shaft. '''bearing-note''' (bãr′ing-nōt), ''n.'' In tuning tempered instruments, like the pianoforte, one of the notes that are first carefully tuned as a basis in tuning the others. Also called ''bearing.'' '''bearing-rein''' (bãr′ing-rān), ''n.'' The rein by which the head of a horse is held up in driving. '''bearing-robe''' (bãr′ing-rōb), ''n.'' A garment answering the same purpose as a bearing-cloth. It was formerly customary for the sponsors to present such a robe to the child. '''bearish''' (bãr′ish), ''a.'' [< ''bear''2 + ''-ish''1.] '''1.''' Partaking of the qualities of a bear; morose or uncouth in manner. {{smaller block|In our own language we seem to allude to this degeneracy of human nature when we call men, by way of reproach, sheepish, ''bearish,'' etc. {{right|''Harris'', Three Treatises, Notes, p. 344.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|bearing|492|beast’s-bane}}</noinclude>{{nop}}{{smaller block|Transactions which have . . . direct ''bearings'' on freedom, on health, on morals, on the permanent well-being of the nation, can never be morally indifferent.
{{right|''Rae'', Contemp. Socialism, p. 213.}}}}
'''5.''' The special meaning or application of anything said or written.
{{smaller block|To change the ''bearing'' of a word.
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, cxxviii.}}}}
'''6.''' The act or capability of producing or bringing forth: as, a tree past ''bearing''.
{{smaller block|In travail of his ''bearing'', his mother was first dead.
{{right|''Robert of Gloucester.''}}}}
'''7.''' In ''arch.'', the space between the two fixed extremes of a beam or timber, or between one extreme and a supporter: that is, its unsupported span.—'''8.''' In ''mach.'', the part in contact with which a journal moves; that part of a shaft or an axle which is in contact with its supports; in general, the part of any piece where it is supported, or the part of another piece on which it rests.—'''9.''' Same as ''bearing-note''.—'''10.''' ''pl.'' In ''ship-building'', the widest part of a vessel below the plank-sheer; the line of flotation which is formed by the water on her sides when upright, with provisions, stores, etc., on board in proper trim.—'''11.''' In ''her.'', any single charge of a coat of arms; any one of the ordinaries, or any heraldic bird, beast, or other figure (see ''charge''); hence, in the plural, the whole heraldic display to which a person is entitled. See ''arm''<sup>2</sup>, 7.—'''12.''' The direction or point of the compass in which an object is seen, or the direction of one object from another, with reference to the points of the compass. {{smaller|In ''geol.'' and ''mining'', used in speaking either of the outcrop of the strata or of the direction of any metalliferous lode or deposit, whether under ground or at the surface: nearly synonymous with ''run'', ''course'', and ''strike''.}}
{{smaller block|“Before the sun could go his own length, the little water will be in the big.” . . .
“I thought as much,” returned the scout, . . . “from the course it takes, and the ''bearings'' of the mountains.”
{{right|''Cooper'', Last of the Mohicans, xxxii.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Antifriction bearing.''' See ''antifriction.''—'''Conical bearing,''' an end-bearing for the spindle of a machine-tool, formed by abutting the spindle-end against the end of a screw. One of these ends is brought to a conical point, and the other is correspondingly countersunk. The screw serves to adjust the bearings for wear.—'''Continuous bearings.''' See ''continuous.''—'''Sand-bearings,''' in ''molding'', the supports for the core in the sand of a mold.—'''Side bearings of a car-truck,''' plates, blocks, or rollers placed on each side of the center-pin to prevent a too great rocking motion.—'''To bring a person to his bearings,''' to put him in his proper place; take him down.—'''To lose one’s bearings,''' to become uncertain or confused in regard to one’s position; become bewildered or puzzled.—'''To take bearings,''' to ascertain on what point of the compass an object lies. The term is also applied to ascertaining the situation or direction of any object estimated with reference to some part of a ship, as on the beam, before the beam, abaft the beam, etc. Hence, to determine one’s position; make one’s self acquainted with the locality in which one is; discover how matters stand; get rid of bewilderment or misunderstanding.}}
{{smaller block|The best use that we can now make of this occasion, it seems to me, is to look about us, ''take'' our ''bearings'', and tell the fugitives . . . what course, in our opinion, they should pursue.
{{right|''W. Phillips'', Speeches, p. 76.}}}}

'''bearing''' (bãr′ing), ''a.'' '''1.''' Supporting; sustaining: as, a ''bearing'' wall or partition (that is, a wall or partition supporting another).—'''2†.''' Solid; substantial: as, “a good ''bearing'' dinner,” ''Fletcher'', Women Pleased, ii. 2.

{{smaller block|<poem>We’ll bait thy bears to death,

{{smaller block|Those who worke with them co’mand them as our ''bearewards'' do the beares, with a ring through the nose, and a cord.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Oct. 21, 1644.}}}}

{{smaller block|I entreated a ''bearward'' one day to come down with the dogs of some four parishes that way.

'''bear-whelp''' (bãr′hwelp), ''n.''   [< ME. ''bere-hwelp''; < ''bear''<sup>2</sup> + ''whelp''.]   The whelp of a bear.

{{smaller block|An unlicked ''bear-whelp''. {{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., iii. 2.}}}}

'''bearwood''' (bãr′wu̇d), ''n.'' The ''Rhamnus Purshiana'', a shrub or small tree of the Pacific States. See ''bearberry'', 2.

'''bearwort''' (bãr′wėrt), ''n.'' The mew or baldmoney, ''Meum athamanticum''.

'''beast''' (bēst), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''beest'', < ME. ''beeste'', ''beste'', < OF. ''beste'', F. ''bête'' = Sp. Pg. It. ''bestia'' = D. LG. ''beest'', < L. ''bestia'', an animal, including all animals except man.]   '''1.''' A living being; an animal: in this extended sense now only in dialectal or colloquial use.

<poem>These ben the eyryssh [airish] ''bestes'', lo.
{{right|''Chaucer'', House of Fame, l. 932.}}</poem>

<poem>To keepe this worlde bothe more and lesse
A skylfull ''beeste'' [man] than will y make.
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 15.}}</poem>

'''2.''' Any four-footed animal, as distinguished from fowls, insects, fishes, and man: as, ''beasts'' of burden; ''beasts'' of the chase; ''beasts'' of the forest. It is applied chiefly to large animals.

{{smaller block|The ''beasts'', the fishes, and the winged fowls.
{{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>One deep cry
Of great wild ''beasts.''</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Palace of Art.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Beasts of chase'' are the buck, the doe, the fox, the marten, and the roe. ''Beasts of the forest'' are the hart, the hind, the hare, the boar, and the wolf. ''Beasts of warren'' are the hare and cony.
{{right|''Cowell'', Law Dictionary.}}}}
'''3.''' Any irrational animal, as opposed to ''man'', as in the phrase ''man and beast'', where ''beast'' usually means horse.
{{smaller block|<poem>O heaven! a ''beast'', that wants discourse of reason,
Would have mourn’d longer.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 2.}}}}
'''4.''' ''pl.'' In ''rural economy'', originally all domestic animals, but now only cattle; especially, fatting cattle as distinguished from other animals.—'''5.''' In a limited specific use, a horse: as, my ''beast'' is tired out. [Local, Scotland and U. S. Compare ''creature'', ''critter'', similarly used.]—'''6.''' Figuratively, a brutal man; a person rude, coarse, filthy, or acting in a manner unworthy of a rational creature.
{{smaller block|<poem>What an afflicted conscience do I live with,
And what a ''beast'' I am grown!</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Valentinian, iv. 1.}}}}
'''7†.''' [In this use also spelled as orig. pron., ''bāste'', < F. ''beste'', now ''bête'', in same sense.] (''a'') An old game of cards resembling loo. (''b'') A penalty or forfeit at this game, and also in ombre and quadrille.—'''Beast royal,''' {{smaller|the lion: used also of the constellation Leo.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And yet ascending was the ''beste roial'',
The gentil Leon with his Aldiran.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Squire’s Tale, l. 256.}}}}
{{smaller block|'''Blatant beast.''' See ''blatant.''}}

'''beasted''' (bēs′ted), ''a.''   [< ''beast'', ''n.'', 7, + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.]   Beaten at ombre or quadrille.

'''beastee''', ''n.'' See ''bheesty.''

'''beastie'''<sup>2</sup> (bēs′ti), ''n.'' See ''bheesty.''

'''2†.''' Absence of reason; stupidity.
{{smaller block|''Beastliness'' and lack of consideration. {{right|''North.''}}}}

'''beastly''' (bēst′li), ''a.''   [< ME. ''beestely'', ''bestely'', ''beastliche''; < ''beast'' + ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1†.''' Natural; animal: the opposite of ''spiritual.''
{{smaller block|It is sowun a ''beestli'' bodi; it shal ryse a spiritual bodi.
{{right|''Wyclif'', 1 Cor. xv. 44.}}}}
'''2.''' Like a beast in form or nature; animal. {{smaller block|''Beastly'' divinities and droves of gods.{{right|''Prior.''}}}}

'''3.''' Like a beast in conduct or instincts; brutal; filthy; coarse.

{{smaller block|Thou art the ''beastliest'', crossest baggage that ever man met withal!{{right|''Middleton (and others)'', The Widow, i. 2.}}}}

'''4.''' Befitting a beast; unfit for human use; filthy; abominable.

{{smaller block|Lewd, profane, and ''beastly'' phrase.{{right|''B. Jonson.''}}}}

{{smaller block|Thrown into ''beastly'' prisons.{{right|''Dickens'', Hist. of Eng., xvi.}}}}

'''5.''' Nasty; disagreeable: as, ''beastly'' weather. [Slang.]

{{smaller block|By laying the defeat to the account of “this ''beastly'' English weather, you know.”{{right|''American'', VI. 245.}}}}

='''Syn.''' ''Brutal'', ''Bestial'', etc. See ''brute''.

'''beastly†''' (bēst′li), ''adv.''   [< ''beast'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.]   In the manner of a beast; filthily; abominably.

{{smaller block|Fie on her! see how ''beastly'' she doth court him.{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., iv. 2.}}}}

<poem>I have seen a handsome cause so foully lost, sir,
So ''beastly'' cast away, for want of witnesses.</poem>{{right|''Fletcher'', Spanish Curate, iii. 1.}}

'''beastlyhead†''' (bēst′li-hed), ''n.''   [< ''beastly'' + ''-head'' = ''-hood''; one of Spenser’s artificial words.]   The character or quality of a beast; beastliness: used by Spenser as a greeting to a beast.

<poem>Sicke, sicke, alas! and little lack of dead,
But I be relieved by your ''beastlyhead''.</poem>{{right|''Spenser'', Shep. Cal., May.}}

'''beast’s-bane''' (bēsts′bān), ''n.'' A variety of the wolf’s-bane, ''Aconitum Lycoctonum''.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
